title: Number of completed tasks exceeds total tasks in PySpark
question:
I have the following (simplified) code running in PySpark.

df is a PySpark dataframe with 2B rows. I keep hitting resource issues when running such a large dataframe, so I'm trying to get a subset of the dataframe to work on.

df_10M = df.limit(10000000)
df_a = df_10M.withColumn(...).withColumn(...).withColumn(...).withColumn(...)
df_a = df_a.drop("oldColA", "oldColB")
df_a.show(10)

When I run this on Jupyter Notebook, I eventually see

[Stage 4:====================(1572 + 12 / 1122)]

1122 should be the total number of tasks, 1572 should be the number of completed tasks, and 12 is the number of running tasks. If I leave the code running, eventually, I hit the Pod ephemeral local storage usage limit.

My question is how can the number of completed tasks be larger than the total number of tasks?
answer:
I’m pretty sure what you’re seeing concerns how Spark handles task retries and speculative execution.

Even though the UI says there are 1122 tasks, it’s possible to see more completed, like your 1572, because Spark will retry tasks if they fail for any reason (memory pressure, executor issues, etc.). Each of those retries counts as a new task attempt, even though it’s technically the same task.

Also, Spark has this thing called speculative execution. If it notices a task lags behind the others, it might spin up a second copy of that task somewhere else. Whichever one finishes first gets used, but both attempts still get counted in the completed total.

So yeah, it looks weird, but that’s just how Spark works under the hood.

If you’re hitting storage limits, you might want to avoid using .limit() — it’s not optimized for large datasets because it doesn’t take partitioning into account. Using .sample() instead is usually more efficient when you just want a smaller slice of a big dataset, like your 2 billion rows.

You could also try disabling speculative execution if it’s causing too many duplicate tasks:

spark.conf.set("spark.speculation", "false")

And if memory’s tight, maybe persist to disk instead of memory with:

df.persist(StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY)
